Two cases of New World screwworm have been confirmed in Starr and Zapata counties, according to state Sen. Judith Zaffirini, KGNS reported.

In response, the Texas Department of Agriculture established Infested Zone 29, covering portions of Jim Hogg, Starr, and Zapata counties in South Texas, and outlined an adjacent surveillance zone. Residents and agricultural producers are urged to report suspected cases promptly.

The confirmed cases put the parasitic fly, which infests the wounds of warm-blooded animals, on South Texas' doorstep — Zapata County borders Webb County to the south. Webb County ranchers and livestock owners should watch their animals for signs of screwworm and report anything suspicious.

Update — November 12, 2026

The Texas Animal Health Commission expanded the state's screwworm infested zone to 25 counties on November 10, adding Bandera, Medina, Irion, and Reagan counties under new executive director orders, according to TAHC data tracked by The County Road. Bandera and Medina had been released from the zone on September 16. TAHC reported 71 confirmed premises across 24 Texas counties as of November 11, up from 68 across 22 counties on November 9. The newest detections include a horse in Bandera County, cattle in Reagan County, and a sheep in Val Verde County, Texas Public Radio reported November 9. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported 126 confirmed animal cases nationwide as of November 9, with 63 still active. The South Texas cases in Starr and Zapata counties reported in this story remain the closest detections to Webb County, and no case has been confirmed in Webb County.

Sources: KGNS; Texas Public Radio (KTTZ), Nov. 9, 2026; Texas Animal Health Commission data via The County Road screwworm tracker, Nov. 11–12, 2026.

title: Two Screwworm Cases Confirmed in Starr, Zapata Counties
